rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wine and gambling involve great sin alongside benefits: wine gives pleasure and trading profit, while gambling can yield money without labor.
rows.anchor: أما في الخمر فما يحصل من اللذة بشربها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although sin is ascribed to wine and gambling themselves, it means drinking wine and gambling, since sin cannot literally be the substances.
rows.anchor: غيرهما، فلا بد من إضمار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation places the sin in consequences of drinking, including neglecting prayer, obscenity, enmity, and hatred.
rows.anchor: ترك الصلاة وقول الفحش والعداوة والبغضاء الذي يحدث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The direct reading is stronger: the sin is attached to wine and gambling, not their consequences, which may not occur even though the sin remains.
rows.anchor: لا بما يحدث عنده، ولأنه قد ينفك من تلك الأمور

rows.speaker: الربيع والضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Rabiʿ and al-Dahhak say the benefits were present before prohibition and the sin after prohibition.
rows.anchor: المنافع قبل التحريم، والإثم بعد التحريم، عن الربيع والضحاك.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view holds that benefit and sin coexist in one state, while prohibition is a separate matter, as water benefits a fasting person if he drinks it.
rows.anchor: في حالة واحدة، وتحريمه ثانية، وإن كان لو شرب انتفع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their sin outweighs their benefit because of the punishment entailed; this is true of every reprehensible thing whose sin exceeds its benefit.
rows.anchor: بما يلزم عليه من العقوبة، وكذلك حال كل قبيح

rows.speaker: ابن عباس وقتادة وعطاء والسدي
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas, Qatada, ʿAtaʾ, and al-Suddi gloss al-ʿafw as surplus beyond one's own and family's needs, given from comfortable means.
rows.anchor: ليكون عن ظهر غنى، عن ابن عباس وقتادة وعطاء والسدي.

rows.speaker: الحسن وعطاء
rows.claim: Al-Hasan and ʿAtaʾ interpret al-ʿafw as a moderate amount, avoiding both extravagance and stinginess.
rows.anchor: الوسط من غير سرف ولا تقتير، عن الحسن وعطاء.

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid interprets al-ʿafw as the obligatory alms.
rows.anchor: وقيل الصدقة المفروضة، عن مجاهد.

rows.speaker: الربيع
rows.claim: Al-Rabiʿ interprets al-ʿafw as what is wholesome or good.
rows.anchor: الطيب، عن الربيع كذلك يبين الله لكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase may mean that God explains proofs concerning spending, wine, and gambling.
rows.anchor: في أمر النفقة والخمر والميسر، وقيل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view takes the explained signs as all the ordinances of Islam.
rows.anchor: في سائر شرائع الإسلام لعلكم تتفكرون

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One interpretation urges people to consider worldly and afterlife needs, keeping enough for livelihood and spending the rest for the hereafter.
rows.anchor: ما يصلحكم من معاشكم، وتنفقون الباقي لآخرتكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another interpretation contrasts the world's passing nature and mixed troubles with the lasting, unalloyed hereafter, urging obedience and avoidance of sin.
rows.anchor: في الدنيا وزوالها وفنائها، وما يشوبها من الهموم

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abu Muslim says the reflection concerns the pleasures of this world and the reward of the hereafter.
rows.anchor: في نعيم الدنيا وثواب الآخرة، عن أبي مسلم.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse's legal discussion is organized around wine and its analogues, gambling, spending, and the verse's proofs.
rows.anchor: في الآية أحكام وأدلة من وجوه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Wine is unquestionably forbidden: it was once permitted, prohibition is necessarily known as part of the religion, its denier is an unbeliever, and its drinker a sinner.
rows.anchor: وعلم ذلك من دينه ضرورة حتى يكفر جاحده، ويفسق شاربه.

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Hasan and a group say this verse prohibited wine; al-Qadi chooses this view because calling it a great sin implies prohibition.
rows.anchor: قال الحسن وجماعة: حرمت بهذه الآية، وهو اختيار القاضي

rows.speaker: قتادة وأبو علي
rows.claim: Qatada and Abu ʿAli say wine was prohibited by the verse in al-Maʾida.
rows.anchor: وقال قتادة وأبو علي: إنما حرمت بآية المائدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Reports from some early authorities say intoxicants were prohibited by the command not to approach prayer while intoxicated; a long report also records some Companions withholding judgment.
rows.anchor: وأن السكر حرم بقوله: (لا تقربوا الصلاة وأنتم سكارى)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-Qadi rejects that timing account: a great sin must be forbidden, this verse is more emphatic than a simple prohibition, and any Companion hesitation could await a stronger ruling.
rows.anchor: قال القاضي: وهذا لا يصح؛ لأن ما فيه إثم كبير

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة وجماعة من العلماء
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa and a group define wine as grape juice that ferments, boils, and throws up foam; they agree that this is wine.
rows.anchor: هو عصير العنب إذا اشتد وغلا وقذف بالزبد عن أبي حنيفة وجماعة من العلماء

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafiʿi defines wine as any drink whose large quantity intoxicates, so even a small quantity counts as wine.
rows.anchor: ما أسكر كثيره فقليله خمر، وهو مذهب الشافعي.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The grape-specific definition is stronger: a Prophetic report distinguishes wine itself from intoxication in other drinks, and the grape definition has consensus while the broader one lacks proof.
rows.anchor: والأول أصح لحديث النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم -: حرمت الخمر لعينها

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: The Prophet is cited as saying that wine is forbidden for its own essence, while intoxication is forbidden from every drink.
rows.anchor: لحديث النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم -: حرمت الخمر لعينها، والسكر من كل شراب

rows.speaker: ابن علية وبشر المريسي
rows.claim: Ibn ʿUlayya and Bishr al-Marisi say cooked grape juice becomes lawful after even minimal cooking.
rows.anchor: إذا طبخ أدنى طبخة حل، عن ابن علية وبشر المريسي

rows.speaker: جماعة
rows.claim: Another group says cooked grape juice is lawful once half of it has evaporated.
rows.anchor: إذا ذهب نصفه حل، عن جماعة

rows.speaker: أبو حنيفة وأبو يوسف وسفيان الثوري وجماعة
rows.claim: Abu Hanifa, Abu Yusuf, Sufyan al-Thawri, and others permit it when two-thirds have evaporated and one-third remains; this is also reported from several early authorities.
rows.anchor: ذهب ثلثاه وبقي ثلثه، وهو مذهب أبي حنيفة وأبي يوسف وسفيان الثوري

rows.speaker: محمد ومالك والشافعي
rows.claim: Muhammad, Malik, and al-Shafiʿi hold that any drink, raw or cooked, is forbidden in small amounts if large amounts intoxicate.
rows.anchor: ما أسكر كثيره فقليله حرام، ويستوي فيه النيء والمطبوخ، عن محمد ومالك والشافعي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The author's school classifies drinks as grape-based, date- or raisin-based, and all other drinks.
rows.anchor: الأشربة على ثلاثة أنواع: الأول العنبي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Grape wine cannot be bought, sold, or drunk; the Prophet is reported to have cursed ten persons connected with wine.
rows.anchor: الخمر، وقد بينا حدها، ولا يجوز بيعها

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A report from the Prophet says that ten people connected with wine are cursed.
rows.anchor: المروي عن النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم - أنه لعن في الخمر عشرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Among other grape drinks, juice cooked briefly cannot be drunk or sold; the half-cooked type may be sold but not drunk, while reducing it by two-thirds permits sale and drinking subject to the stated exception for amusement and intoxication.
rows.anchor: ما طبخ أدنى طبخة لا يحل شربه ولا بيعه، والمنصف يجوز بيعه

rows.speaker: الشافعي
rows.claim: Al-Shafiʿi holds that any drink intoxicating in large quantities is forbidden even in a small amount.
rows.anchor: وقال الشافعي: ما أسكر كثيره فقليله خمر حرام.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's leading people out of unbelief is explained as assistance, facilitation, command, and encouragement, since the act of leaving is the servant's own and merits reward.
rows.anchor: على التسهيل والمعونة والأمر به والحث عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage refutes the Compulsionists: they say God, rather than Satan, moves unbelievers from faith to unbelief, but the verse attributes this to Satan and censures him.
rows.anchor: وتدل على بطلان مذهب المجبرة في المخلوق والاستطاعة والإرادة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse establishes allegiance to believers and disavowal of the misguided: God is the believers' guardian and does not ally with unbelievers.
rows.anchor: وجوب موالاة المؤمنين، والبراءة من أهل الضلالة

rows.speaker: الأعمش وحمزة
rows.claim: The common reading has rabiya with a fatḥa on the yāʾ because of the following alif; al-Aʿmash and Hamza read the yāʾ quiescent, following the original form.
rows.anchor: وعن الأعمش وحمزة ربي بسكون الياء على الأصل

rows.speaker: القراء
rows.claim: The readers generally pronounce buhita with ḍamma on bāʾ and kasra on hāʾ, in the passive; some read both vowels fatḥa, making Abraham the stunned subject.
rows.anchor: والقراء على بهت بضم الباء، وكسر الهاء

rows.speaker: أبو جعفر ونافع
rows.claim: Abu Jaʿfar and Nafiʿ lengthen the alif in ana before a following alif in phrases such as ana uḥyī; other readers omit it in connected speech and retain it at pause.
rows.anchor: وقرأ أبو جعفر ونافع أنا أحيي بمد أنا

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muḥājja is a reciprocal verbal form derived from proof: each disputant acts or speaks in response to the other's action or statement.
rows.anchor: مفاعلة من الحجة، ووزنه فاعل كقاتل وخاصم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shams is feminine and its plural is shumus.
rows.anchor: والشمس: جمعها شموس، وهي تؤنث.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Baht can mean confronting someone with a lie; it also means bewilderment when proof prevails, and has three reported vocalizations.
rows.anchor: مواجهة الرجل بالكذب عاتبه، بهته بهتا، ومنه الحديث

rows.speaker: النبي
rows.claim: A Prophetic report describes the Jews as a people of falsehood or bewildering speech, illustrating the word baht.
rows.anchor: ومنه الحديث: اليهود قوم بهت والبهت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase al-ladhī kafara occupies nominative position because the verb is annexed to it.
rows.anchor: الذي كفر موضعه رفع لإضافة الفعل إليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The preposition ilā in ilā alladhī ḥāj is an expression of wonder, as in asking whether one has seen such conduct.
rows.anchor: دخلت في قوله إلى الذي حاج للتعجيب كما يقال

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After establishing God as believers' protector and saying unbelievers have no protector, God consoles the Prophet with Abraham's story as further proof.
rows.anchor: لما بين تعالى أنه ولي المؤمنين وناصرهم، وأن الكافر لا ولي له

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The address to Muhammad expresses wonder: have you seen the conduct of someone who disputed and argued?
rows.anchor: ألم تر يا محمد تعجيب منه لنبيه، أي أرأيت كصنع من حاج

rows.speaker: مجاهد
rows.claim: Mujahid, Qatada, and al-Rabiʿ identify Abraham's disputant as Nimrod son of Canaan, the first to claim divinity.
rows.anchor: النمرود بن كنعان، وهو أول من تجرأ وادعى الربوبية، عن مجاهد وقتادة والربيع

rows.speaker: مقاتل
rows.claim: Muqatil places the dispute after Abraham broke the idols but before he was thrown into the fire.
rows.anchor: عند كسر الأصنام قبل الإلقاء في النار، عن مقاتل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another account places the dispute after Abraham had been thrown into the fire.
rows.anchor: وقيل: بعد إلقائه في النار

rows.speaker: الحسن وأبو علي وأبو مسلم
rows.claim: Hasan, Abu ʿAli, and Abu Muslim take the pronoun as Nimrod: God gave him worldly wealth and dominion, which even an unbeliever may receive, unlike spiritual authority.
rows.anchor: آتاه قيل: تعود إلى المحاج أعطاه الله الملك وهو نعيم الدنيا

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abu Muslim also says the ruler was given dominion while a believer and later became an unbeliever.
rows.anchor: وقيل: آتاه الملك وكان مؤمنا فكفر، عن أبي مسلم

rows.speaker: أبو حذيفة وأبو القاسم
rows.claim: Abu Hudhayfa and Abu al-Qasim take the pronoun in atāhu to refer to Abraham.
rows.anchor: وقيل: تعود الكناية على إبراهيم، عن أبي حذيفة وأبي القاسم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An omitted question is understood before Abraham's answer: someone asks who his Lord is, and he replies that his Lord gives life and death.
rows.anchor: كأنه قيل: من ربك؟ فقال: ربي الذي يحيي ويميت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nimrod claims to give life by releasing a condemned prisoner and to cause death by killing whomever he chooses.
rows.anchor: أنا أحيي بالتخلية من الحبس من وجب عليه القتل، وأميت بالقتل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nimrod's answer is profound ignorance: he equivocates on the wording and avoids the proof, since only God originates life and death.
rows.anchor: وهذا جهل عظيم منه؛ لأنه اعتمد في المعارضة الاشتراك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham asks Nimrod to bring the sun from the west after God brings it from its place of rising to its setting.
rows.anchor: يعني من موضع الطلوع فأت بها من المغرب موضع الغروب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham's shift to the sun argument was not a concession: Nimrod had no response to the first proof, and the new proof reinforced it.
rows.anchor: إلى حجة أخرى لا عجزا، ولكن ظهرت حجته من غير اعتراض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation says Abraham moved from one example to another because the core proof is that God can do what no one else can, such as life, death, or celestial motion.
rows.anchor: وقيل: انتقل من مثال إلى مثال؛ لأن أصل الحجة أنه يقدر على ما لا يقدر عليه أحد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nimrod did not challenge Abraham to ask God to bring the sun from the west because he knew from the signs that God would do it, making his defeat worse.
rows.anchor: لأنه علم بما رأى من الآيات أنه لو سأله لفعله، فيزداد فضيحة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Alternatively, God abandoned Nimrod and gave Abraham subtle aid, preventing the opponent from confusing the issue or offering a specious doubt.
rows.anchor: خذله ولطف لإبراهيم حتى لم يلبس، ولم يأت بشبهة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unbeliever was bewildered and silenced when the proof appeared.
rows.anchor: تحير وانقطع عند ظهور الحجة

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abu Muslim says the disputant remained defeated, unable to say anything.
rows.anchor: بقي مغلوبا لا يجد مقالا، عن أبي مسلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading is that God does not assist wrongdoers in achieving corrupt aims.
rows.anchor: بالمعونة على بلوغ البغية من الفساد

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another reading is that God does not guide them in argument as He guides His prophets.
rows.anchor: لا يهديهم إلى المحاجة كما يهدي أنبياءه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further view says God withholds subtle aid and support from people known to be ineligible for it.
rows.anchor: إذ علم أنه لا لطف لهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations say God does not judge them to be guided or lead them to Paradise.
rows.anchor: لا يحكم بهدايتهم، وقيل: لا يهديهم إلى الجنة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The validity of disputation shows that knowledge of God is acquired rather than necessary, since debating necessary truths would be improper.
rows.anchor: تدل الآية على أن المعارف مكتسبة غير ضرورية؛ لذلك صحت المحاجة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse refutes blind imitation as a route to knowledge: if imitation produced knowledge, disputation would be unnecessary.
rows.anchor: وتدل على بطلان التقليد؛ إذ لو كان طريقا للعلم لما احتيج إلى المحاجة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The argument validates analogy and rational inference because they make disputation possible.
rows.anchor: وتدل على صحة القياس والاستدلال؛ لأن المحاجة بها تتم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nimrod's claim to give life and death indicates that he claimed divinity for himself.
rows.anchor: هذا الذي حاج كان يدعي الربوبية لنفسه؛ لذلك قال: أنا أحيي وأميت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The route to knowing God is to infer from acts no one else can perform; the verse uses life and death as especially clear examples.
rows.anchor: الطريق إلى معرفته سبحانه - هو فعل ما لا يقدر عليه غيره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Nimrod's reply was an obviously false equivocation: Abraham argued from origination, while Nimrod answered with a verbal resemblance, so he went silent.
rows.anchor: احتج بالاختراع، فعارضه بالعبارة، فلذلك سكت عن الجواب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Giving a second proof after the first succeeds is sound reinforcement; Abraham changes examples, not the underlying proof that only God can create such acts.
rows.anchor: حسن إيراد حجة بعد حجة تأكيدا إذا ظهرت الأولى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham chose life-giving because it indicates God and is the first and foundational blessing, reminding Nimrod and others of divine unity and favor.
rows.anchor: وإنما اختار إبراهيم (عليه السلام) الإحياء؛ لأنه - مع دلالته

rows.speaker: ابن عباس
rows.claim: Ibn ʿAbbas counts the trials as forty shares, including ten in al-Muʾminun and ten from Sāʾil Sāʾil, along with the preceding ten.
rows.anchor: فجعلها أربعين سهما، عن ابن عباس.

rows.speaker: قتادة والربيع وابن عباس
rows.claim: Qatada, al-Rabiʿ, and Ibn ʿAbbas say Abraham was tested by being commanded to perform the pilgrimage rites.
rows.anchor: أمره بمناسك الحج، عن قتادة والربيع وابن عباس.

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan says Abraham's seven trials were the sun, moon, stars, circumcision, sacrificing his son, the fire, and migration; he fulfilled them all.
rows.anchor: ابتلاه بسبعة أشياء: بالشمس، والقمر، والكواكب، والختان، وذبح ابنه، والنار، والهجرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view identifies the trials with the following verses, including God's promise to make Abraham a leader.
rows.anchor: ابتلاؤه بالآيات التي بعدها إني جاعلك للناس إماما

rows.speaker: أبو القاسم
rows.claim: Abu al-Qasim narrows the trial to God's statement that Abraham would be made a leader, which Abraham undertook to fulfill.
rows.anchor: هو قوله: إني جاعلك للناس إماما فتكفل بذلك، عن أبي القاسم

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu ʿAli says Abraham was commanded to convey certain words to his community; the author considers this the strongest view, while allowing all these accounts.
rows.anchor: أمره بكلمات يؤديهن إلى أمته، فقام بذلك، عن أبي علي. والكل محتمل

rows.speaker: الحسن
rows.claim: Al-Hasan explains Abraham completed the trials as fulfilling them.
rows.anchor: فأتمهن قيل: وفى بهن، عن الحسن

rows.speaker: قتادة والربيع
rows.claim: Qatada and al-Rabiʿ explain completion as carrying out the trials fully.
rows.anchor: وقيل: عمل بهن على التمام، عن قتادة والربيع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Abraham asks that some of his descendants be leaders whom people follow; another view takes his request as asking that his offspring remain on his religion.
rows.anchor: إبراهيم ومن ذريتي أي اجعل من ذريتي من يؤتم به

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The prayer for descendants to follow Abraham's religion is linked to his prayer that God keep him and his sons from idol worship; God says unjust descendants will not share his covenant.
rows.anchor: وقيل: إنه سأل لعقبه أن يكونوا على عهده ودينه

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu ʿAli says Abraham asked God to inform him whether a prophet would be raised among his children.
rows.anchor: هو سؤال منه لله تعالى أن يعرفه أن في ولده من يبعثه نبيا

rows.speaker: السدي وأبو علي
rows.claim: Al-Suddi and Abu ʿAli interpret God's covenant as prophethood.
rows.anchor: النبوة، عن السدي وأبي علي

rows.speaker: مجاهد وأبو حذيفة
rows.claim: Mujahid and Abu Hudhayfa interpret God's covenant as leadership or imamate.
rows.anchor: الإمامة، عن مجاهد وأبي حذيفة

rows.speaker: عطاء
rows.claim: ʿAtaʾ interprets the covenant as God's mercy.
rows.anchor: وقيل: رحمتي عن عطاء، وقيل: طاعتي

rows.speaker: الضحاك
rows.claim: Al-Dahhak interprets the covenant as obedience to God.
rows.anchor: طاعتي، عن الضحاك

rows.speaker: أبو عبيدة
rows.claim: Abu ʿUbayda interprets the covenant as God's promise.
rows.anchor: أماني، عن أبي عبيدة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The unjust are those who wrong themselves through disobedience to God; the unqualified word is one of blame.
rows.anchor: من ظلم نفسه بمعصية الله تعالى، وهو عند الإطلاق اسم ذم

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: The verse shows God answered Abraham by placing prophethood and scripture among his descendants; otherwise the reply would simply deny his request or exclude all descendants.
rows.anchor: قال أبو علي: الآية دالة على أنه سيعطي بعض ولده

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The created heavens and earth require a maker because they are originated and subject to temporal events.
rows.anchor: كونها مخلوقة محدثة، ولا بد من محدث إذا لم يخل من الحوادث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their measured, coherent arrangement points to a wise and knowing governor.
rows.anchor: كونها مقدرة محكمة متسقة فتدل على مدبر حكيم عليم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their beneficial design—the raised sky, useful sun and moon, spread earth, and plants—points to a wise creator.
rows.anchor: تتكامل بها المصلحة من رفع السماء والانتفاع بالشمس والقمر، ودحو الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The immense heavens and earth remain suspended without support or place through a capable maker, as affirmed by another verse.
rows.anchor: سكونهما من غير علاقة، ولا مكان مع ثقلهما وعظمهما لا يصح إلا من صانع قادر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The regular paths of stars and orbits maintain human livelihood, daily life, and reckoning, pointing to divine governance.
rows.anchor: أحوال النجوم السائرات والأفلاك الدائرات على طريقة واحدة مما يتم به مصالح الخلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The contrast of night and day, light and darkness, cannot be produced by bodies themselves and therefore requires an originator unlike them.
rows.anchor: نقيض ما صار به الليل والنهار من الضياء والظلام؛ إذ لا يقدر عليه أحد من الأجسام

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their regular succession enables human interests, knowledge of years and months, rest, and seeking livelihood.
rows.anchor: جريهما على طريقة واحدة حتى تتم به المصالح ومعرفة الأزمنة من السنين والشهور

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The increasing and decreasing lengths of night and day, and each one's taking from the other, are among the signs.
rows.anchor: أخذ أحدهما من صاحبه والزيادة والنقصان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Night and day depend on the sun and moon following their appointed courses.
rows.anchor: تعلق ذلك بجري الشمس والقمر على الحد الذي يجري عليه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their duration varies with the differing eastern and western horizons of the earth.
rows.anchor: قصر كل واحد وطوله باختلاف مشارق الأرض ومغاربها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their alternation serves human welfare; perpetual night or day would prevent it.
rows.anchor: اختلافهما حتى لو دام أحدهما واتصل لما تمت المصلحة ومنافع الخلق

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Without the alternation of day and night, people could not know years or keep reckoning.
rows.anchor: لولاهما لما صح شيء من معرفة السنين والحساب

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Although ships are built by human beings, their construction depends on materials such as wood and iron that God supplies.
rows.anchor: فأما الفلك وإن كان من أفعال العباد فلا يتم إلا بأمور من جهته تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ships can sail because God gives water its fluid quality.
rows.anchor: صفة الماء في الرقة التي لولاها لما صح جري الفلك

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their movement also depends on the powerful current and forces and moisture God places in water.
rows.anchor: ما يفعله تعالى في الماء من الجرية الشديدة وما فيه من الاعتمادات والرطوبات

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The passage consoles the Prophet and his Companions amid persecution and deaths, since hearing of earlier righteous people encourages them to endure similar trials.
rows.anchor: ما فيه تسلية للنبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم - وأصحابه فيما نالهم من الكفار بما جرى من قتل

rows.speaker: الفراء
rows.claim: Al-Farraʾ glosses the opening as a question: Have you thought?
rows.anchor: معناه أحسبتم، عن الفراء

rows.speaker: الزجاج
rows.claim: Al-Zajjaj instead takes the opening as a transition meaning rather, you thought.
rows.anchor: بل حسبتم، عن الزجاج

rows.speaker: الأصم
rows.claim: Al-Asamm says believers imagined that affirming the Messenger without serving and worshipping God would be enough to enter Paradise.
rows.anchor: تصدقوا الرسول دون أن تكونوا دعاة لله عابدين له، عن الأصم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view says Paradise cannot be attained without deserving it and bearing hardship; believers must endure trials as earlier believers did.
rows.anchor: بغير استحقاق وتحمل المشاق، كلا بل يحصل بتحمل المشاق في الله تعالى

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One reading treats ma in lammā as an extra particle, equivalent here to lam; a parallel uses the phrase about later followers not yet joining.
rows.anchor: قيل: ولم يأتكم، و(ما): صلة كقوله: (وآخرين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase is explained either as the description or the likeness of those who passed before the believers.
rows.anchor: أي صفة من مضى من قبلكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another explanation says the believers had not yet faced afflictions like those of earlier generations and calls them to patient endurance.
rows.anchor: لما يأتكم من البلايا ما أتاهم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those who passed before are the prophets and believers who came earlier.
rows.anchor: مضوا من قبلكم من النبيين والمؤمنين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One explanation glosses al-baʾsāʾ as poverty and hardship, and al-ḍarrāʾ as illness and chronic affliction.
rows.anchor: البأساء الفقر والشدة، والضراء: المرض والزمانة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view includes religious hardships such as war, leaving family and property, and expulsion.
rows.anchor: ما تعلق بمضار الدين من حرب وخروج من الأهل والمال وإخراج

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The people were shaken by different kinds of hardship; another explanation says fear of the enemy distressed them.
rows.anchor: حركوا بأنواع البلايا، وقيل: أزعجوا بالخوف من العدو

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Their distress became so intense that the Messenger and believers asked when God's promised aid would come.
rows.anchor: حتى يقول الرسول والذين آمنوا معه متى نصر الله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The question is an appeal to hasten the promised victory, like the appeal of a person undergoing a trial.
rows.anchor: استعجال للموعود كما يفعله الممتحن

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abu Muslim says the Prophet and believers both ask when help will come and reassure themselves that it is near.
rows.anchor: كلاهما من كلام النبي - صلى الله عليه وسلم - والمؤمنين ثقة بالنصرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another parsing states the believers ask when victory will come and the Prophet answers that it is near, as another verse distributes rest to night and seeking bounty to day.
rows.anchor: وقالوا - يعني المؤمنين -: متى نصر الله؟ فقال الرسول: قريب، كقوله: (جعل لكم الليل والنهار

rows.speaker: الأصم وأبو علي
rows.claim: Al-Asamm and Abu ʿAli say the Prophet and believers ask when help will come, then God promises that it is near.
rows.anchor: قال الرسول والمؤمنون: متى نصر الله؟ فقال الله تعالى: نصره قريب، فهو وعده تعالى

rows.speaker: أبو عمرو
rows.claim: Abu ʿAmr reads yaʿmalūn in the third person, warning the previously mentioned opponents; the other readers use the second-person form, addressing Muslims with a promise for obedience.
rows.anchor: قرأ أبو عمرو يعملون بالياء وعيدا لمن سبق ذكرهم من المخالفين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Shatr means toward or in the direction of, a sense explained earlier.
rows.anchor: الشطر: النحو، وقد مضى ذكره

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ghāfil means lacking knowledge or awareness.
rows.anchor: والغفلة: ذهاب العلم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The common Quraysh form of ḥaythu has yāʾ and nominative marking; other analyses call it built on ḍamma like mundhu or nominative by extension, and other dialects use fatḥa or wāw.
rows.anchor: حيث): بالياء والرفع لغة قريش، وقراءة العامة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After explaining the qibla for residents, the verse addresses travel and removes the idea that the direction changes between travel and residence, despite concessions for voluntary prayer on a mount.
rows.anchor: لما بين تعالى أمر قبلة الحاضرين بين أحوال السفر، فقال تعالى: ومن حيث خرجت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Al-ḥaqq may mean the commanded qibla; it may instead mean an established rule that will not be abrogated, like the description of God as the Real.
rows.anchor: قيل: القبلة المأمور بها، ويحتمل أنه الثابت

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God knows their circumstances and will recompense them; the statement promises believers and threatens unbelievers because nothing is hidden from Him.
rows.anchor: وهو وعد للمؤمنين ووعيد للكافرين أنه لا يخفى عليه شيء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Tabdīl means changing something by putting another in its place; badal is an object placed in place of another.
rows.anchor: التبديل: تغيير الشيء بوضع غيره موضعه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse about the earth being changed into another earth illustrates the word badal.
rows.anchor: يوم تبدل الأرض غير الأرض

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in baddalahu can refer to the will as the act of bequeathing, to the bequest's contents, to its written wording, or to the preceding command.
rows.anchor: الهاء في قوله: بدله يرجع إلى الوصية؛ لأنه بمنزلة الإيصاء

rows.speaker: المفضل
rows.claim: Al-Mufaddal says the pronoun refers to the written record because a testament is a statement.
rows.anchor: الوصية قول، فلذلك ذكر الكتابة عن المفضل

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The pronoun in ithmuhu points to the act of changing, which is implied by the verb baddalahu.
rows.anchor: يرجع على التبديل المدلول عليه بقوله: فمن بدله

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After mentioning the testament, God warns against altering it.
rows.anchor: لما ذكر تعالى الوصية عقبها بذكر الوعيد في تغييرها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The one who changes a testament alters what the testator ordered after hearing it from the testator, witnesses, or guardians; liability follows knowledge and hearing.
rows.anchor: بدل الوصية وغيرها عما أوصى بعد ما سمعه من الموصي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: One view assigns the sin to the executor.
rows.anchor: إثم التبديل على الذين يبدلونه قيل: الوصي

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another view assigns the sin to the witness.
rows.anchor: قيل: الوصي، وقيل: الشاهد، وقيل: الجميع

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A further view includes everyone who heard the testament.
rows.anchor: وقيل: الجميع؛ لأنهم دخلوا في أنهم سمعوا ذلك

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu ʿAli says God hears all sounds and knows all things.
rows.anchor: سميع لجميع المسموعات عليم بجميع المعلومات، عن أبي علي

rows.speaker: الأصم
rows.claim: Al-Asamm says God hears their testimony and knows what they do.
rows.anchor: وقيل: سميع لشهادتهم، عليم بما يعملون، عن الأصم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Other explanations say God hears the testament and knows its character, hears whether the testator spoke justly or unjustly, and knows whether the executor corrects or changes it.
rows.anchor: سميع للوصية، عليم بصفتها، لا يخفى عليه شيء منها

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Another gloss says God hears people's wills and knows their intentions.
rows.anchor: سميع لوصاياكم عليم بنياتكم

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse assigns punishment only to the person who performs the act, refuting punishment of unbelievers' children and punishment without sin.
rows.anchor: العقوبة لا يستحقها إلا من يتولى العمل، فيبطل قول المجبرة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse refutes the claim that a dead person is punished when an executor fails to carry out the will or pay its debts.
rows.anchor: إن الميت يعذب إذا قصر الوصي في تنفيذ وصاياه

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Executors and witnesses are forbidden to alter a testament by adding, subtracting, redirecting, sharing, or changing its stated attributes.
rows.anchor: حظر التبديل من الوصي والشاهد، وذلك يكون بزيادة أو نقصان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Placing the birds on the mountains illustrates resurrection: as the birds answered Abraham's call, people will answer God's call from every region of earth.
rows.anchor: مثل ضربه الله تعالى له كما أنه دعا الطيور فأجابته كذلك أراد الله البعث

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Saʿyan is explained as running quickly or as walking on their legs, the latter making the proof more striking; flight is rejected because birds are not said to saʿā when flying.
rows.anchor: قيل: عدوا، وقيل: مشيا عنى أرجلهن

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An interpretation as flying is rejected, since birds are not said to saʿā when flying.
rows.anchor: لا يقال للطير: سعى إذا طار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: An alternative reading supplies omitted actions: Abraham cut them apart, called, and they answered and came to him.
rows.anchor: ففي الكلام حذف، وهو أنه قطع ودعا فأجبن وأتين

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: A report says each part returned to its whole and blood and feathers rejoined the pieces until each bird lived and walked.
rows.anchor: كان بصير إلى جملته، وكل دم وريش يصير إلى الأجزاء

rows.speaker: أبو علي
rows.claim: Abu ʿAli glosses the Mighty as capable of everything and the Wise as knowing how to revive the dead and perfect His creation.
rows.anchor: حكيم عالم بإحياء الميت وإحكام صنعه، عن أبي علي

rows.speaker: أبو مسلم والأصم
rows.claim: Abu Muslim and al-Asamm say the Mighty is one to whom all things submit, while the Wise acts with wisdom and rightness.
rows.anchor: حكيم فعله حكمة وصواب، عن أبي مسلم والأصم

rows.speaker: عاصم وابن عامر وأبو جعفر ويعقوب
rows.claim: ʿAsim, Ibn ʿAmir, Abu Jaʿfar, and Yaʿqub read the verbs with nominative endings; the other readers use the jussive, while Ibn ʿAbbas is reported with the accusative.
rows.anchor: قرأ فيغفر ويعذب برفع الراء والباء عاصم وابن عامر وأبو جعفر ويعقوب

rows.speaker: أبو العباس والأخفش
rows.claim: Abu al-ʿAbbas and al-Akhfash parse the nominative as a new sentence, meaning that He forgives; it may also express the consequence of the reckoning.
rows.anchor: عن أبي العباس والأخفش كأنه قيل: فهو يغفر

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The jussive reading coordinates forgiveness and punishment with the jussive verb yuḥāsibkum.
rows.anchor: وأما الجزم فبالعطف على (يحاسبكم)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The accusative may coordinate with the verbal noun of the first verb, estimating a conditional reckoning, or may contain an implied an.
rows.anchor: تقديره: إن يكن محاسبة فيغفر لمن يشاء

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ibdāʾ means making something public or visible.
rows.anchor: الإبداء: الإعلان والإظهار

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Ikhfāʾ means concealment.
rows.anchor: والإخفاء: الكتمان

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Qadīr and qādir have the same basic meaning, but qadīr is more emphatic because of its morphological form.
rows.anchor: وقدير وقادر بمعنى إلا أن في (قدير) مبالغة

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The lām indicates ownership: God owns the heavens and earth and controls their use, destruction, and restoration.
rows.anchor: لام الملك يعني له ملكهما، أي يملك تصريفهما

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the conditional construction, tabdū and takhfū are jussive, and yuḥāsibkum is jussive as the condition's response.
rows.anchor: و (إن) حرف جزاء، و(تبدوا)

rows.speaker: الأصم
rows.claim: Al-Asamm says that after listing the sūra's ordinances, the passage concludes with admonition, monotheism, submission, and judgment to deter disobedience.
rows.anchor: لما فرغ من بيان القرائض والشرائع المذكورة في السورة ختم بالموعظة

words: لِلَّهِ مَا فِى ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَمَا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ
rows.speaker: أبو مسلم
rows.claim: Abu Muslim links God's ownership of heaven and earth to the prior statement that He knows everything: nothing can be hidden from such an owner.
rows.anchor: لما قال: والله بكل شيء عليم أتبعه بقوله: لله ما في السماوات

words: لِلَّهِ مَا فِى ٱلسَّمَٰوَٰتِ وَمَا فِى ٱلْأَرْضِ
rows.speaker: القاضي
rows.claim: Al-Qadi links the verse to the preceding financial safeguards: God prescribes them for people's benefit, since He already owns everything.
rows.anchor: لما أمر تعالى بهذه الوثائق صيانة للأموال واحتياطا بين أنه إنما تعبد بذلك

words: وَإِن تُبْدُوا۟ مَا فِىٓ أَنفُسِكُمْ أَوْ تُخْفُوهُ
rows.speaker: الشعبي وعكرمة ومجاهد
rows.claim: Al-Shaʿbi, ʿIkrima, and Mujahid connect the verse to the warning against concealing testimony: God owns all things and will repay concealment and disclosure.
rows.anchor: لما نهى عن كتمان الشهادة وأوعد عليها بين أن له ملك السماوات والأرض
